## ART — Fine Arts

### ART.1 — Art History, Aesthetic Philosophy & Christian Worldview

#### ART.1.1 — Aesthetic Philosophy & Christian Thought

##### ART.1.1.1 — Art as Worship & Service

- `ART.1.1.1.1` Identify making art as a way to say 'Thank You' to God.
- `ART.1.1.1.2` Name making a card for a sick friend as service.
- `ART.1.1.1.3` Recall that God sees our work.
- `ART.1.1.1.4` Observe art in the church.
- `ART.1.1.1.5` Summarize how art can help people pray.
- `ART.1.1.1.6` Explain 'Soli Deo Gloria' (Glory to God alone).
- `ART.1.1.1.7` Compare showing off vs. serving.
- `ART.1.1.1.8` Identify talents as things to be shared.
- `ART.1.1.1.9` Analyze the function of art in the Tabernacle/Temple.
- `ART.1.1.1.10` Interpret the concept of 'vocation' (calling).
- `ART.1.1.1.11` Connect excellence in craft to honoring God.
- `ART.1.1.1.12` Explain how secular work can be worship.
- `ART.1.1.1.13` Construct a vision for artistic vocation.
- `ART.1.1.1.14` Evaluate the distinction between 'Christian Art' and 'Art by Christians'.
- `ART.1.1.1.15` Defend the value of art that does not explicitly preach.
- `ART.1.1.1.16` Synthesize service to neighbor with artistic expression.

##### ART.1.1.2 — Biblical Foundations for Art (creativity as imago Dei)

- `ART.1.1.2.1` Identify God as the first Artist (Creation).
- `ART.1.1.2.2` Name ourselves as made in His image.
- `ART.1.1.2.3` Recall that we like to make things because God makes things.
- `ART.1.1.2.4` Observe the colors God used in the world.
- `ART.1.1.2.5` Summarize the story of Bezalel (first artist filled with the Spirit).
- `ART.1.1.2.6` Explain 'Imago Dei' (Image of God).
- `ART.1.1.2.7` Compare making something from nothing (God) vs. something from something (Us).
- `ART.1.1.2.8` Identify creativity as a gift.
- `ART.1.1.2.9` Analyze Tolkien's concept of 'Sub-creation'.
- `ART.1.1.2.10` Interpret Exodus 31 regarding skill and intelligence in art.
- `ART.1.1.2.11` Connect the Incarnation to the validity of physical art.
- `ART.1.1.2.12` Explain the Dominion Mandate applied to culture.
- `ART.1.1.2.13` Construct a biblical theology of the arts.
- `ART.1.1.2.14` Evaluate the historical iconoclasm in the church.
- `ART.1.1.2.15` Defend the material world as good (anti-Gnostic).
- `ART.1.1.2.16` Synthesize the Cultural Mandate with the Great Commission.

- `ART.1.1.5.12` Explain why beauty matters.
- `ART.1.1.5.13` Construct a philosophical argument for objective beauty.

- `ART.1.1.5.15` Defend the Christian view that beauty reflects God's nature.
- `ART.1.1.5.16` Synthesize aesthetics with theology.

##### ART.1.1.7 — The Problem of the Ugly (modernism, realism)

- `ART.1.1.7.1` Identify that not all pictures are pretty.
- `ART.1.1.7.2` Name a sad picture.
- `ART.1.1.7.3` Recall that sad things are true too.
- `ART.1.1.7.4` Observe a picture of a storm or battle.
- `ART.1.1.7.5` Summarize why an artist might paint something ugly (to tell the truth).

- `ART.1.1.7.7` Compare a perfect princess picture with a real girl picture.
- `ART.1.1.7.8` Identify emotions in 'ugly' art.
- `ART.1.1.7.9` Analyze the Grotesque in art history.
- `ART.1.1.7.10` Interpret the use of dissonance and distortion.
- `ART.1.1.7.11` Connect the Fall to the presence of ugliness.

- `ART.1.1.7.13` Construct a theology of the 'Ugly' in art.
- `ART.1.1.7.14` Evaluate the gratuity vs. necessity of disturbing imagery.
- `ART.1.1.7.15` Defend the Cross as the ultimate example of redemptive ugliness.
- `ART.1.1.7.16` Synthesize the tension between the 'already' and 'not yet' in aesthetics.

#### ART.1.3 — Principles of Art Criticism

##### ART.1.3.1 — Analysis (How is it organized?)

- `ART.1.3.1.1` Identify lines that point to things.
- `ART.1.3.1.2` Name the most important part (Focal Point).
- `ART.1.3.1.3` Recall patterns.
- `ART.1.3.1.4` Observe if the picture feels balanced.
- `ART.1.3.1.5` Summarize how the artist moves your eye.
- `ART.1.3.1.6` Explain the use of contrast (light vs. dark).
- `ART.1.3.1.7` Compare the background and foreground.
- `ART.1.3.1.8` Identify the mood created by colors.
- `ART.1.3.1.9` Analyze the Principles of Design (Balance, Rhythm, Unity).
- `ART.1.3.1.10` Interpret the compositional structure.
- `ART.1.3.1.11` Connect the technique to the effect.
- `ART.1.3.1.12` Explain color relationships.
- `ART.1.3.1.13` Construct a formal analysis of a masterwork.
- `ART.1.3.1.14` Evaluate the success of the composition.
- `ART.1.3.1.15` Defend the artist's choices.
- `ART.1.3.1.16` Synthesize the relationship between form and content.

- `ART.1.3.3.7` Describe the texture.
- `ART.1.3.3.8` Identify the setting.
- `ART.1.3.3.9` Analyze the literal qualities of the work.
- `ART.1.3.3.10` Interpret the technical skill involved.
- `ART.1.3.3.11` Connect vocabulary words to the description.

##### ART.1.3.5 — Judgment (Is it good? Why?)

- `ART.1.3.5.1` Decide if you like it.

## BIB — Bible & Theology

### BIB.1 — Apologetics and Worldviews

#### BIB.1.1 — Classical Apologetics

##### BIB.1.1.1 — Arguments for God’s Existence

- `BIB.1.1.1.1` Identify that God made the world because it is beautiful and ordered.
- `BIB.1.1.1.2` Name God as the First Maker (everything needs a maker).
- `BIB.1.1.1.3` Recall that the world didn't happen by accident.
- `BIB.1.1.1.4` Observe that a watch needs a watchmaker, and the world needs a Creator.
- `BIB.1.1.1.5` Summarize the idea of Cause and Effect (The Universe has a Cause).
- `BIB.1.1.1.6` Explain the Argument from Design (Complexity implies intelligence).
- `BIB.1.1.1.7` Compare a building (needs a builder) to the universe (needs a Creator).
- `BIB.1.1.1.8` Apply the Moral Argument: We know right and wrong because God exists.
- `BIB.1.1.1.9` Analyze the Kalam Cosmological Argument (Everything that begins to exist has a cause).
- `BIB.1.1.1.10` Interpret the Fine-Tuning Argument (anthropic principle).
- `BIB.1.1.1.11` Connect the existence of objective moral values to a Moral Lawgiver.
- `BIB.1.1.1.12` Explain why an infinite regress of causes is impossible.
- `BIB.1.1.1.13` Construct a formal defense using the Ontological Argument (Anselm/Plantinga).
- `BIB.1.1.1.14` Evaluate Leibniz's Argument from Contingency (Why is there something rather than nothing?).
- `BIB.1.1.1.15` Defend theism against the 'God of the Gaps' objection.
- `BIB.1.1.1.16` Synthesize Classical arguments to build a cumulative case for theism.

##### BIB.1.1.2 — Natural Theology

- `BIB.1.1.2.1` Identify that the sky and trees tell us God is strong.
- `BIB.1.1.2.2` Name 'General Revelation' as God speaking through nature.
- `BIB.1.1.2.3` Recall that everyone knows there is a God (Romans 1).
- `BIB.1.1.2.4` Observe God's power in a storm or a mountain.
- `BIB.1.1.2.5` Summarize Psalm 19 ('The heavens declare the glory of God').
- `BIB.1.1.2.6` Explain that nature shows God exists, but not how to be saved.
- `BIB.1.1.2.7` Compare what we learn from a sunset vs. what we learn from the Bible.
- `BIB.1.1.2.8` Apply the truth that no one has an excuse for ignoring God.
- `BIB.1.1.2.9` Analyze the limits of Natural Theology (cannot reveal the Trinity or Atonement).
- `BIB.1.1.2.10` Interpret Romans 1:18-20 regarding the suppression of truth.
- `BIB.1.1.2.11` Connect the order of the universe to the mind of God (Logos).
- `BIB.1.1.2.12` Explain the relationship between Reason and Revelation.
- `BIB.1.1.2.13` Construct a historical overview of Natural Theology (Aquinas to Paley).
- `BIB.1.1.2.14` Evaluate the impact of Darwinism on the Argument from Design.
- `BIB.1.1.2.15` Defend the compatibility of Faith and Reason.
- `BIB.1.1.2.16` Produce an essay on the necessity of Special Revelation to complete General Revelation.

#### BIB.1.2 — Cults and Unique Systems

##### BIB.1.2.1 — Christianity vs Other Worldviews (Secularism)

- `BIB.1.2.1.1` Identify that God made the world, it wasn't an accident.
- `BIB.1.2.1.2` Name 'Secular' as living like God isn't there.
- `BIB.1.2.1.3` Recall that we are made for a purpose.
- `BIB.1.2.1.4` Observe that people are sad without God.
- `BIB.1.2.1.5` Summarize what an Atheist believes (No God).
- `BIB.1.2.1.6` Explain that if there is no God, there is no real right or wrong.
- `BIB.1.2.1.7` Compare living for 'now' with living for eternity.
- `BIB.1.2.1.8` Apply the hope we have in Jesus.
- `BIB.1.2.1.9` Analyze the worldview of Materialism (only matter exists).
- `BIB.1.2.1.10` Interpret the logical end of Atheism (Nihilism/Meaninglessness).
- `BIB.1.2.1.11` Connect Darwinian evolution to the devaluation of human life.
- `BIB.1.2.1.12` Explain Postmodernism (No absolute truth).

- `BIB.1.2.1.14` Evaluate the problem of evil for the Atheist (no standard of 'good').
- `BIB.1.2.1.15` Defend the necessity of God for meaning, value, and purpose.
- `BIB.1.2.1.16` Synthesize the Christian worldview as the only one that fits reality.

##### BIB.1.2.2 — Major Cults (Mormonism/LDS, Jehovah's Witnesses)

- `BIB.1.4.1.15` Defend the faith by showing that non-Christian systems collapse on their own terms.
- `BIB.1.4.1.16` Synthesize the 'reductio ad absurdum' method in apologetics.

- `BIB.1.4.2.1` Identify that numbers and logic come from God.

##### BIB.1.4.3 — Worldviews and Ultimate Authorities

- `BIB.1.4.3.4` Observe that some people don't believe the Bible.

- `BIB.1.4.3.6` Explain that everyone has faith in something (God or themselves).
- `BIB.1.4.3.7` Compare the Christian view (God made us) with the Secular view (we are accidents).
- `BIB.1.4.3.8` Apply the Bible as the starting point for thinking.
- `BIB.1.4.3.9` Analyze the concept of a 'Presupposition' (an assumption taken for granted).
- `BIB.1.4.3.10` Interpret the myth of neutrality (no one is neutral).
- `BIB.1.4.3.11` Connect the fear of the Lord to the beginning of knowledge.
- `BIB.1.4.3.12` Explain why evidence alone doesn't convince everyone (Romans 1).
- `BIB.1.4.3.13` Construct a diagram of the 'Archimedean Point' (Ultimate Authority).
- `BIB.1.4.3.14` Evaluate why Empiricism and Rationalism fail as ultimate standards.
- `BIB.1.4.3.15` Defend the necessity of the Christian worldview to make sense of anything.
- `BIB.1.4.3.16` Synthesize the relationship between circular reasoning and ultimate authorities.

### BIB.2 — Biblical Literacy & Foundation

#### BIB.2.1 — Biblical Narrative Structure

##### BIB.2.1.1 — The Metanarrative: Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration

- `BIB.2.1.1.1` Identify that God made the world good.
- `BIB.2.1.1.2` Name the sad day when Adam and Eve disobeyed.
- `BIB.2.1.1.3` Recall that Jesus came to rescue us.
- `BIB.2.1.1.4` Observe that one day God will make everything new.
- `BIB.2.1.1.5` Summarize the four main parts of the Bible's big story.
- `BIB.2.1.1.6` Explain why we need a Rescuer (because of the Fall).
- `BIB.2.1.1.7` Compare the Garden of Eden with the New Jerusalem.
- `BIB.2.1.1.8` Apply the hope of Restoration to a bad day.
- `BIB.2.1.1.9` Analyze how individual Bible stories fit into the larger arc.
- `BIB.2.1.1.10` Interpret the 'Proto-evangelium' (Gen 3:15) as the first promise of Redemption.
- `BIB.2.1.1.11` Connect the Fall to the brokenness seen in the world today.
- `BIB.2.1.1.12` Explain the consistency of God's plan from Genesis to Revelation.
- `BIB.2.1.1.13` Construct a diagram of the meta-narrative timeline.
- `BIB.2.1.1.14` Evaluate other worldviews against the linear history of Scripture.
- `BIB.2.1.1.15` Defend the necessity of a historical Fall for the logic of the Gospel.
- `BIB.2.1.1.16` Synthesize the believer's role in the current 'Redemption' phase.

##### BIB.2.1.2 — The Covenants: Adamic, Noahic, Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New

- `BIB.2.1.2.1` Identify a promise as something special you keep.
- `BIB.2.1.2.2` Name the rainbow as God's promise to Noah.
- `BIB.2.1.2.3` Recall that God promised Abraham a big family.
- `BIB.2.1.2.4` Observe that God never breaks a promise.
- `BIB.2.1.2.5` Summarize God's promise to David (a King forever).
- `BIB.2.1.2.6` Explain the difference between a rule (Law) and a promise (Covenant).
- `BIB.2.1.2.7` Compare the Old Covenant (Stone tablets) with the New Covenant (Heart).
- `BIB.2.1.2.8` Identify the signs of the covenants (Rainbow, Circumcision, Sabbath, Cup).
- `BIB.2.1.2.9` Analyze the conditional vs. unconditional nature of specific covenants.
- `BIB.2.1.2.11` Connect the Abrahamic promise to the coming of Christ.
- `BIB.2.1.2.12` Explain how the Mosaic covenant showed our sin.
- `BIB.2.1.2.13` Construct a chart tracing the progressive revelation of the covenants.
- `BIB.2.1.2.14` Evaluate Covenant Theology vs. Dispensationalism (introductory).
- `BIB.2.1.2.15` Defend the unity of the Covenant of Grace across the ages.
- `BIB.2.1.2.16` Synthesize Christ as the mediator and fulfillment of all covenants.

##### BIB.2.1.3 — Typology: Shadows and Substance in Scripture

- `BIB.2.1.3.1` Identify a picture that looks like something real.
- `BIB.2.1.3.2` Name the Passover Lamb.
- `BIB.2.1.3.3` Recall that Noah's Ark saved people, just like Jesus saves us.
- `BIB.2.1.3.4` Observe that the Old Testament points to Jesus.
- `BIB.2.1.3.5` Summarize how the Tabernacle teaches us about God's holiness.
- `BIB.2.1.3.6` Explain what a 'Shadow' is in the Bible (Colossians 2).
- `BIB.2.1.3.7` Compare the Bronze Serpent with Jesus on the Cross (John 3).
- `BIB.2.1.3.8` Identify Joseph as a type of Christ (suffering servant/ruler).
- `BIB.2.1.3.9` Analyze the criteria for a valid biblical type.
- `BIB.2.1.3.10` Interpret the priesthood of Aaron as a type of Christ's priesthood.
- `BIB.2.1.3.11` Connect the Manna in the wilderness to the Bread of Life.
- `BIB.2.1.3.12` Explain the typology of the Temple.
- `BIB.2.1.3.13` Construct a study of the Day of Atonement typology.
- `BIB.2.1.3.14` Evaluate the danger of allegorizing vs. reading typologically.
- `BIB.2.1.3.15` Defend the Christocentric reading of the Old Testament.
- `BIB.2.1.3.16` Synthesize the 'Greater than' pattern (Jesus is the greater Moses/David/Solomon).

##### BIB.2.1.4 — The Kingdom of God: Already and Not Yet

- `BIB.2.1.4.1` Identify Jesus as the King.
- `BIB.2.1.4.2` Name Heaven as God's home.
- `BIB.2.1.4.3` Recall that Jesus is ruling right now.

- `BIB.2.1.4.8` Apply the prayer 'Your Kingdom Come'.

- `BIB.2.1.4.10` Interpret the miracles as breaking-in of the Kingdom.
- `BIB.2.1.4.11` Connect the Resurrection to the start of the New Creation.
- `BIB.2.1.4.12` Explain the tension of living between the times.
- `BIB.2.1.4.13` Construct a theology of Christian engagement in culture.
- `BIB.2.1.4.14` Evaluate the error of over-realized eschatology (expecting perfection now).
- `BIB.2.1.4.15` Defend the spiritual nature of the Kingdom vs. political expectations.
- `BIB.2.1.4.16` Synthesize the hope of the final consummation with present faithfulness.

#### BIB.2.2 — New Testament Overview

##### BIB.2.2.1 — The Synoptic Problem and John's Unique Perspective

- `BIB.2.2.1.1` Identify Matthew, Mark, and Luke as three books that tell similar stories.
- `BIB.2.2.1.2` Name John as the fourth story about Jesus.
- `BIB.2.2.1.3` Recall that they all tell the truth about Jesus.
- `BIB.2.2.1.4` Observe that John talks a lot about 'Love' and 'Light'.
- `BIB.2.2.1.5` Summarize why the first three are called 'Synoptic' (seen together).
- `BIB.2.2.1.6` Explain that John focuses on who Jesus is (God).
- `BIB.2.2.1.7` Compare a story in Mark with the same story in Luke.
- `BIB.2.2.1.8` Identify the 'I AM' statements in John.
- `BIB.2.2.1.9` Analyze the literary relationship between Matthew, Mark, and Luke.
- `BIB.2.2.1.10` Interpret the Prologue of John (The Word was God).
- `BIB.2.2.1.11` Connect the distinct audiences (Jews vs. Gentiles) to the gospel variations.
- `BIB.2.2.1.12` Explain the priority of Mark (common theory).

- `BIB.2.2.1.14` Evaluate the unique theological contribution of John's Gospel.
- `BIB.2.2.1.15` Defend the reliability of having four distinct witnesses.
- `BIB.2.2.1.16` Synthesize the four-fold portrait of Christ (King, Servant, Man, God).

##### BIB.2.2.2 — The History of the Early Church (Acts)

- `BIB.2.2.3.1` Identify a letter in the Bible.

- `BIB.2.2.3.15` Defend the authority of the Apostles' letters as Scripture.

#### BIB.2.4 — Systematic Reading of Scripture

##### BIB.2.4.1 — Daily Reading Habits (Consistency)

- `BIB.2.4.1.1` Identify the Bible as God's special book that should be opened every day.
- `BIB.2.4.1.2` Observe a parent or teacher reading the Bible and imitate the posture of listening.
- `BIB.2.4.1.3` Name specific times of the day (morning or night) when we can hear from God.
- `BIB.2.4.1.4` Ask to hear stories from the Bible as part of a daily routine.
- `BIB.2.4.1.5` Explain why reading the Bible daily is food for the Christian soul.
- `BIB.2.4.1.6` Apply a simple checklist to track reading the Bible for a full week.
- `BIB.2.4.1.7` Compare the habit of Bible reading to other daily habits like brushing teeth or eating.
- `BIB.2.4.1.8` Summarize the main thought of a short daily passage in a journal.
- `BIB.2.4.1.9` Analyze personal schedules to identify obstacles to consistent Bible reading.
- `BIB.2.4.1.10` Connect the practice of daily reading to the concept of 'abiding' in Christ (John 15).
- `BIB.2.4.1.11` Explain the difference between reading for information and reading for transformation.
- `BIB.2.4.1.12` Evaluate different times of day to determine when personal focus is highest for reading.
- `BIB.2.4.1.13` Construct a sustainable, long-term plan for reading through the entire Bible.
- `BIB.2.4.1.14` Evaluate the spiritual impact of inconsistency and develop strategies for discipline.
- `BIB.2.4.1.15` Defend the necessity of daily Scripture intake against the cultural pressure of busyness.
- `BIB.2.4.1.16` Synthesize daily reading habits with deep study to produce a holistic view of Scripture.

##### BIB.2.4.2 — Inductive Bible Study Overview

- `BIB.2.4.2.1` Observe what is happening in a picture of a Bible story.
- `BIB.2.4.2.2` Ask 'Who?', 'What?', and 'Where?' questions about a story.
- `BIB.2.4.2.3` Identify the main person in the story.
- `BIB.2.4.2.4` Retell what happened in the beginning, middle, and end.
- `BIB.2.4.2.5` Summarize the three steps: Observation, Interpretation, Application.
- `BIB.2.4.2.6` Apply specific color codes to mark key words in a printed text.
- `BIB.2.4.2.7` Explain why we must look at what the text says before what it means.
- `BIB.2.4.2.8` Compare the characters in a story to understand their choices.
- `BIB.2.4.2.9` Analyze a paragraph by circling key words, listing facts, and noting contrasts.
- `BIB.2.4.2.10` Interpret the meaning of a passage based only on the observations made.
- `BIB.2.4.2.11` Connect the interpretation to a specific, actionable application.
- `BIB.2.4.2.12` Explain the danger of jumping to application without proper observation.
- `BIB.2.4.2.13` Construct a full inductive study of a New Testament epistle (Observation, Interpretation, Application).
- `BIB.2.4.2.14` Evaluate different commentaries to check personal interpretation.
- `BIB.2.4.2.15` Perform independent research on historical background to aid observation.
- `BIB.2.4.2.16` Produce a teaching outline based on the inductive study of a passage.

##### BIB.2.4.3 — Memorization and Meditation (Puritan Practice)

- `BIB.2.4.3.1` Memorize short key verses (e.g., Genesis 1:1, John 3:16).
- `BIB.2.4.3.2` Repeat a verse out loud until it can be said without help.
- `BIB.2.4.3.3` Identify a verse that brings comfort when afraid.
- `BIB.2.4.3.4` Copy a memory verse in best handwriting.
- `BIB.2.4.3.5` Memorize longer passages or sets of verses (e.g., The Beatitudes, Psalm 23).
- `BIB.2.4.3.6` Explain the meaning of a memorized verse in own words.
- `BIB.2.4.3.7` Apply a memorized verse to a specific temptation or struggle.
- `BIB.2.4.3.8` Compare the difference between just knowing the words and thinking about them (meditation).
- `BIB.2.4.3.9` Analyze a memorized passage by breaking it down phrase by phrase.
- `BIB.2.4.3.10` Connect memorized verses to other parts of the Bible to support a doctrine.
- `BIB.2.4.3.11` Explain the Puritan concept of 'chewing' on the Word (meditation) for spiritual nourishment.
- `BIB.2.4.3.12` Research the context of a memory verse to ensure it is applied correctly.
- `BIB.2.4.3.13` Construct a system for retaining and reviewing memorized Scripture over time.
- `BIB.2.4.3.14` Evaluate the role of meditation in fighting sin and cultivating joy.
- `BIB.2.4.3.15` Produce a written meditation on a passage, exploring its implications deeply.
- `BIB.2.4.3.16` Defend the discipline of 'hiding God's Word in the heart' as essential for spiritual warfare.

##### BIB.2.4.4 — Reading for Devotion (Piety and Application)

- `BIB.2.4.4.1` Identify what a Bible story teaches us about God's love.
- `BIB.2.4.4.2` Ask, 'What does God want me to do?' after hearing a story.
- `BIB.2.4.4.3` Copy a short verse that helps us trust Jesus.
- `BIB.2.4.4.4` Express thanks to God for the truth found in His Word.
- `BIB.2.4.4.5` Apply a specific command from Scripture to a situation at school or home.
- `BIB.2.4.4.6` Explain how a passage encourages us to love God or love our neighbor.
- `BIB.2.4.4.7` Summarize what a text reveals about God's character (e.g., He is holy, He is kind).
- `BIB.2.4.4.8` Participate in a guided prayer based on a Psalm.
- `BIB.2.4.4.9` Analyze own heart responses to Scripture (conviction, comfort, or confusion).
- `BIB.2.4.4.10` Connect the truths of a passage to personal struggles and doubts.
- `BIB.2.4.4.11` Explain how the Holy Spirit uses the Word to change our hearts.
- `BIB.2.4.4.12` Interpret the difference between moralism (being good) and gospel fruit (loving Christ).
- `BIB.2.4.4.13` Evaluate personal life choices in light of specific Scriptural principles.
- `BIB.2.4.4.14` Construct prayers that are saturated with the language and theology of the text read.
- `BIB.2.4.4.15` Produce a devotional reflection that applies deep theological truth to daily life.
- `BIB.2.4.4.16` Defend the practice of reading for relationship over reading for mere academic knowledge.

##### BIB.2.4.5 — Reading for Understanding (Comprehension)

- `BIB.2.4.5.1` Retell the main events of a Bible story in the correct order.
- `BIB.2.4.5.2` Identify the main character in a Bible story.
- `BIB.2.4.5.3` Ask questions about words or ideas in the Bible that are hard to understand.

- `BIB.2.4.5.5` Summarize the 'Who, What, When, Where' of a passage.
- `BIB.2.4.5.6` Explain the plain meaning of a text without adding to it.
- `BIB.2.4.5.7` Categorize a passage as a story, a song, or a rule/command.
- `BIB.2.4.5.8` Compare two different stories to find similarities in how God acts.
- `BIB.2.4.5.9` Analyze a passage to determine the author's main point.
- `BIB.2.4.5.10` Interpret the meaning of key words within their immediate context.
- `BIB.2.4.5.11` Explain the difference between observation (what it says) and interpretation (what it means).
- `BIB.2.4.5.12` Connect a specific passage to the broader context of the chapter.
- `BIB.2.4.5.13` Evaluate a text to determine the author's logical flow and argument.
- `BIB.2.4.5.14` Construct a detailed outline of a biblical chapter or book.
- `BIB.2.4.5.15` Perform independent word studies to clarify the meaning of crucial terms.
- `BIB.2.4.5.16` Produce a written summary of a passage that accurately reflects the author's intent.

##### BIB.2.4.6 — The Lectio Divina Method (Historical Approach)

- `BIB.2.4.6.1` Listen quietly to a short Bible reading.
- `BIB.2.4.6.2` Identify one word or phrase that stands out.
- `BIB.2.4.6.3` Ask God to help understand the special word.
- `BIB.2.4.6.4` Express a simple prayer back to God about the reading.
- `BIB.2.4.6.5` Summarize the four steps: Read, Think, Pray, Rest (Lectio, Meditatio, Oratio, Contemplatio).
- `BIB.2.4.6.6` Apply the method to a short Psalm.
- `BIB.2.4.6.7` Explain what it feels like to listen to God through His Word.
- `BIB.2.4.6.8` Participate in a guided time of quiet reading and prayer.
- `BIB.2.4.6.9` Analyze how slowing down reading helps notice details often missed.
- `BIB.2.4.6.10` Interpret the difference between studying for facts and reading for communion.
- `BIB.2.4.6.11` Connect the historical practice of Lectio Divina to the modern quiet time.
- `BIB.2.4.6.12` Explain how 'chewing' on the text (Meditatio) leads to prayer (Oratio).
- `BIB.2.4.6.13` Evaluate the benefits of contemplative reading in a distracted digital age.
- `BIB.2.4.6.14` Construct a personal rhythm of reading that incorporates silence and reflection.
- `BIB.2.4.6.15` Produce a journal entry documenting the movement from reading to contemplation.
- `BIB.2.4.6.16` Defend the historical validity of this practice within the Protestant tradition.

##### BIB.2.4.7 — Whole-Bible Reading Plans (Discipline)

- `BIB.2.4.7.1` Recall that the Bible has two main parts: the Old Testament and the New Testament.
- `BIB.2.4.7.2` Identify the very first book (Genesis) and the very last book (Revelation).
- `BIB.2.4.7.3` Follow along in a picture Bible as an adult reads through major stories.
- `BIB.2.4.7.4` Name the four Gospels as the stories about Jesus.
- `BIB.2.4.7.5` Categorize Bible books into Law, History, Poetry, Prophecy, Gospels, and Letters.
- `BIB.2.4.7.6` Summarize the general flow of the Bible from Creation to the New Heavens.
- `BIB.2.4.7.7` Apply a reading plan to finish one entire book of the Bible.
- `BIB.2.4.7.8` Compare the length and style of different books (e.g., Psalms vs. Mark).
- `BIB.2.4.7.9` Analyze the structure of a canonical reading plan versus a chronological one.
- `BIB.2.4.7.10` Connect individual books to the larger metanarrative of Scripture.
- `BIB.2.4.7.11` Explain the value of reading the 'whole counsel of God' rather than just favorite verses.
- `BIB.2.4.7.12` Interpret how the Old Testament prepares the way for the New Testament.
- `BIB.2.4.7.13` Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of different reading plans (M’Cheyne, Chronological, etc.).
- `BIB.2.4.7.14` Construct a personalized plan to read the entire Bible in one or two years.
- `BIB.2.4.7.15` Perform independent research to understand the historical setting of the books being read.
- `BIB.2.4.7.16` Produce a synthesis of a major theme traced through a whole-Bible reading.

### BIB.4 — Church History

#### BIB.4.1 — The Early Church (Apostolic to Nicene)

##### BIB.4.1.1 — Heresies of the Early Church

- `BIB.4.1.1.1` Identify a heresy as a lie about God.

- `BIB.4.1.1.9` Analyze the danger of Marcionism (rejecting the Old Testament).

- `BIB.4.1.1.16` Synthesize the importance of 'Orthodoxy' (Right Glory/Belief).

- `CFL.1.1.1.3` Recall that accents tell us where to push the voice.
- `CFL.1.1.1.4` Observe marks moving.

##### DST.4.1.3 — Iterative Testing (failure analysis, refining based on feedback)

- `DST.4.1.3.4` Try again with a new idea.
- `DST.4.1.3.5` Summarize what needs to be changed (Version 2).
- `DST.4.1.3.6` Explain that failure helps us learn.
- `DST.4.1.3.7` Test the model with a specific task.
- `DST.4.1.3.8` Record what happened during the test.
- `DST.4.1.3.9` Analyze the root cause of a failure.
- `DST.4.1.3.10` Interpret feedback to generate improvements.
- `DST.4.1.3.11` Connect iteration to the design cycle.
- `DST.4.1.3.12` Explain 'Optimisation'.
- `DST.4.1.3.13` Construct a testing regime to destruction.
- `DST.4.1.3.14` Evaluate the results of cyclical testing.
- `DST.4.1.3.15` Defend the value of 'failing fast' in innovation.
- `DST.4.1.3.16` Synthesize feedback into a refined final solution.

##### DST.4.1.4 — Prototyping (card modeling, foam mockups, proof-of-concept rigs)

- `DST.4.1.4.1` Build a model with cardboard and tape.
- `DST.4.1.4.2` Identify that the model is not the real thing.
- `DST.4.1.4.3` Use scissors safely.
- `DST.4.1.4.4` Test if the model stands up.
- `DST.4.1.4.5` Construct a 'mock-up' using styrofoam or clay.
- `DST.4.1.4.6` Explain why we make models before the real thing (to save money).
- `DST.4.1.4.7` Use masking tape for temporary joins.
- `DST.4.1.4.8` Create a paper prototype.
- `DST.4.1.4.9` Analyze the fidelity of a prototype (Low-fi vs. Hi-fi).
- `DST.4.1.4.10` Construct a proof-of-concept rig for a mechanism.
- `DST.4.1.4.11` Connect modeling materials (foam board, corriflute) to function.
- `DST.4.1.4.12` Explain rapid prototyping.
- `DST.4.1.4.13` Construct a fully functional high-fidelity prototype.
- `DST.4.1.4.14` Evaluate the aesthetic finish of a presentation model.
- `DST.4.1.4.15` Defend the choice of prototyping method for the stage of design.
- `DST.4.1.4.16` Synthesize digital fabrication with hand finishing.

##### DST.4.1.5 — Sketching Techniques (crating, rendering textures, rapid ideation)

- `DST.4.1.5.1` Draw ideas on paper.
- `DST.4.1.5.2` Use colors to show different parts.
- `DST.4.1.5.3` Label the drawing.
- `DST.4.1.5.4` Draw the object from the front.
- `DST.4.1.5.5` Use 'Crating' (drawing a box first) to draw 3D shapes.
- `DST.4.1.5.6` Sketch an object in Isometric (30 degrees).
- `DST.4.1.5.7` Render simple textures (wood grain, shiny metal).
- `DST.4.1.5.8` Generate multiple quick ideas (ideation).
- `DST.4.1.5.9` Analyze light sources to render shadow and tone.
- `DST.4.1.5.10` Interpret perspective (1-point and 2-point) in sketching.
- `DST.4.1.5.11` Connect thick and thin lines to enhance depth.
- `DST.4.1.5.12` Explain the purpose of annotations.
- `DST.4.1.5.13` Construct professional concept art presentations.
- `DST.4.1.5.14` Evaluate the clarity of communication in sketches.
- `DST.4.1.5.15` Defend the use of analogue sketching in a digital age.
- `DST.4.1.5.16` Synthesize marker rendering with fine liner detailing.

##### DST.4.1.6 — Technical Drawing (Orthographic projection, isometric, exploded views)

- `DST.4.1.6.1` Trace a shape.
- `DST.4.1.6.2` Draw the shape of the object flat.
- `DST.4.1.6.3` Identify the top, front, and side.
- `DST.4.1.6.4` Use a ruler to draw straight lines.
- `DST.4.1.6.5` Draw a shape on isometric grid paper.
- `DST.4.1.6.6` Explain the difference between a 2D plan and a 3D drawing.
- `DST.4.1.6.7` Draw a net (flat pattern) for a box.
- `DST.4.1.6.8` Identify an 'Exploded View' (parts pulled apart).
- `DST.4.1.6.9` Analyze Third Angle Orthographic Projection (standard layout).
- `DST.4.1.6.10` Construct a Front, Plan, and End elevation.
- `DST.4.1.6.11` Connect the views using projection lines.
- `DST.4.1.6.12` Explain the 45-degree transfer line.
- `DST.4.1.6.13` Construct detailed assembly drawings with parts lists.
- `DST.4.1.6.14` Evaluate the accuracy of a sectional view.
- `DST.4.1.6.15` Defend the adherence to ISO/ANSI drawing standards.
- `DST.4.1.6.16` Synthesize geometry and standardization for manufacture.

#### DST.4.2 — Evaluation & Quality Assurance

##### DST.4.2.1 — Commercial Viability (costing, scaling, manufacturing feasibility)

- `DST.4.2.1.1` Count how much money the materials cost.
- `DST.4.2.1.2` Identify that selling price must be higher than making price.
- `DST.4.2.1.3` Recall that time is money.
- `DST.4.2.1.4` Observe price tags.
- `DST.4.2.1.5` Calculate the total cost of materials.
- `DST.4.2.1.6` Explain 'Profit'.
- `DST.4.2.1.7` Compare making one item vs. making many.
- `DST.4.2.1.8` Identify expensive parts.
- `DST.4.2.1.9` Analyze the difference between fixed and variable costs.
- `DST.4.2.1.10` Interpret a break-even chart.
- `DST.4.2.1.11` Connect design complexity to manufacturing time.
- `DST.4.2.1.12` Explain standard components to save money.
- `DST.4.2.1.13` Construct a comprehensive bill of materials (BOM) with costing.
- `DST.4.2.1.14` Evaluate the scalability of a prototype.
- `DST.4.2.1.15` Defend the pricing strategy.
- `DST.4.2.1.16` Synthesize manufacturing feasibility with economic models.

##### DST.4.2.2 — Lifecycle Analysis (assessing environmental impact from cradle to grave)

- `DST.4.2.2.1` Identify if the material can be recycled.
- `DST.4.2.2.2` Name the bin where it goes.
- `DST.4.2.2.3` Recall that trash hurts the earth.
- `DST.4.2.2.4` Observe that things break and get thrown away.
- `DST.4.2.2.5` Summarize where materials come from (trees, oil, mines).
- `DST.4.2.2.6` Explain what happens when we throw it away (Landfill).
- `DST.4.2.2.7` Compare a disposable cup with a reusable one.
- `DST.4.2.2.8` Identify the '6 Rs' (Recycle, Reuse, Reduce, Refuse, Rethink, Repair).
- `DST.4.2.2.9` Analyze the Carbon Footprint of a product.
- `DST.4.2.2.10` Interpret a Lifecycle Assessment (LCA) chart.
- `DST.4.2.2.11` Connect transportation distance to environmental cost.
- `DST.4.2.2.12` Explain 'Built-in Obsolescence'.
- `DST.4.2.2.13` Construct a Cradle-to-Cradle design strategy.
- `DST.4.2.2.14` Evaluate the embodied energy of materials.
- `DST.4.2.2.15` Defend the stewardship of resources in manufacturing.
- `DST.4.2.2.16` Synthesize circular economy principles.

##### DST.4.2.3 — Testing against Design Specifications (objective vs. subjective)

- `DST.4.2.3.1` Check if the object does what we wanted.
- `DST.4.2.3.2` Ask 'Did I finish the job?'.
- `DST.4.2.3.3` Identify if it is strong enough.
- `DST.4.2.3.4` Recall the main rule.
- `DST.4.2.3.5` Check the design against the list of criteria.
- `DST.4.2.3.6` Explain the difference between 'It works' and 'It looks good'.
- `DST.4.2.3.7` Measure the finished product.
- `DST.4.2.3.8` Rate the success out of 10.
- `DST.4.2.3.9` Analyze the difference between Objective (facts) and Subjective (opinion) testing.
- `DST.4.2.3.10` Interpret data from performance tests.
- `DST.4.2.3.11` Connect the evaluation back to the original brief.
- `DST.4.2.3.12` Explain valid testing methods.
- `DST.4.2.3.13` Construct a rigorous testing report comparing metrics to specs.
- `DST.4.2.3.14` Evaluate the validity of the specification itself.
- `DST.4.2.3.15` Defend the success of the project with evidence.
- `DST.4.2.3.16` Synthesize quantitative data with qualitative feedback.

##### DST.4.2.4 — Tolerances & Quality Control (go/no-go gauges, manufacturing accuracy)

- `DST.4.2.4.1` Check if parts fit together.
- `DST.4.2.4.2` Identify if a part is too big or too small.
- `DST.4.2.4.3` Recall that we need to measure carefully.
- `DST.4.2.4.4` Observe that all Lego bricks fit together.
- `DST.4.2.4.5` Summarize why accuracy matters.
- `DST.4.2.4.6` Explain that pieces need to be the right size to work.
- `DST.4.2.4.7` Use a template to check a shape.
- `DST.4.2.4.8` Identify a 'wobbly' joint.
- `DST.4.2.4.9` Analyze the concept of Tolerance (+/- mm).
- `DST.4.2.4.10` Interpret the function of a Go/No-Go gauge.
- `DST.4.2.4.11` Connect quality control to customer satisfaction.
- `DST.4.2.4.12` Explain 'Quality Assurance' vs. 'Quality Control'.
- `DST.4.2.4.13` Construct a quality control plan for batch production.
- `DST.4.2.4.14` Evaluate the capability of a manufacturing process.
- `DST.4.2.4.15` Defend the cost of quality control measures.
- `DST.4.2.4.16` Synthesize statistical process control concepts (intro).

##### DST.4.2.5 — User Trials & Field Testing

- `DST.4.2.5.1` Let a friend play with the toy.
- `DST.4.2.5.2` Watch if they smile.
- `DST.4.2.5.3` Identify if they hold it correctly.
- `DST.4.2.5.4` Ask them if they like it.
- `DST.4.2.5.5` Ask a user to perform a specific task.
- `DST.4.2.5.6` Record how long it takes them.
- `DST.4.2.5.7` Explain why the designer shouldn't explain how to use it (intuitive).
- `DST.4.2.5.8` Gather verbal feedback.
- `DST.4.2.5.9` Analyze user behavior during a trial.
- `DST.4.2.5.10` Interpret body language and frustration points.
- `DST.4.2.5.11` Connect field testing to real-world conditions.
- `DST.4.2.5.12` Explain the value of a 'Beta' test.
- `DST.4.2.5.13` Construct a structured user trial protocol.
- `DST.4.2.5.14` Evaluate the reliability of user feedback.
- `DST.4.2.5.15` Defend design changes based on trial outcomes.
- `DST.4.2.5.16` Synthesize usability heuristics with field data.

#### DST.4.3 — Investigative Research & Analysis

##### DST.4.3.1 — Anthropometrics & Ergonomics (using human measurement data for design)

- `DST.4.3.1.1` Identify that people come in different sizes.
- `DST.4.3.1.2` Test if a handle is comfortable to hold.
- `DST.4.3.1.3` Recall that chairs act as support for our bodies.
- `DST.4.3.1.4` Observe that some things are too big or too small for me.
- `DST.4.3.1.5` Measure hand span or height for a class project.
- `DST.4.3.1.6` Explain what 'Ergonomics' means (fitting the product to the person).
- `DST.4.3.1.7` Design a handle that fits a specific hand size.
- `DST.4.3.1.8` Compare a comfortable tool with an uncomfortable one.
- `DST.4.3.1.9` Analyze the 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles.
- `DST.4.3.1.10` Interpret anthropometric data tables.
- `DST.4.3.1.11` Connect user comfort to safety and efficiency.
- `DST.4.3.1.12` Explain the 'Average User' fallacy.
- `DST.4.3.1.13` Construct a workspace design using rigorous anthropometric data.
- `DST.4.3.1.14` Evaluate the ergonomic risks of a specific design (RSI).
- `DST.4.3.1.15` Defend the exclusion or inclusion of specific percentiles.
- `DST.4.3.1.16` Synthesize biomechanics with product design.

##### DST.4.3.2 — Intellectual Property (patents, copyright, trademarks, design rights)

- `DST.4.3.2.1` Identify my work vs. someone else's work.
- `DST.4.3.2.2` Name a famous logo (e.g., Lego).
- `DST.4.3.2.3` Recall that copying isn't fair.
- `DST.4.3.2.4` Sign my name on my drawing.
- `DST.4.3.2.5` Summarize why inventors protect their ideas.
- `DST.4.3.2.6` Explain what a logo is (Trademark).
- `DST.4.3.2.7` Identify the Copyright symbol ©.
- `DST.4.3.2.8` Compare an original idea with a copy.
- `DST.4.3.2.9` Analyze the difference between a Patent (invention) and Copyright (art/text).
- `DST.4.3.2.10` Interpret the purpose of a Trademark.
- `DST.4.3.2.11` Connect IP theft to ethical stewardship.
- `DST.4.3.2.12` Explain 'Registered Design' rights.
- `DST.4.3.2.13` Construct a patent search for prior art.
- `DST.4.3.2.14` Evaluate the ethical tension between IP protection and open source.
- `DST.4.3.2.15` Defend the moral right of the creator.
- `DST.4.3.2.16` Synthesize legal knowledge with design strategy.

##### DST.4.3.3 — Market Research (identifying gaps, analyzing competitors)

- `DST.4.3.3.1` Look at similar toys in a store.
- `DST.4.3.3.2` Identify what makes a toy special.
- `DST.4.3.3.3` Name the price of an object (concept of money).
- `DST.4.3.3.4` Observe what is popular.
- `DST.4.3.3.5` Compare the prices of similar items.
- `DST.4.3.3.6` Explain why someone might buy one item over another.
- `DST.4.3.3.7` Identify a 'gap' (something missing).
- `DST.4.3.3.8` Collect pictures of competing products.
- `DST.4.3.3.9` Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of competitors (SWOT).
- `DST.4.3.3.10` Interpret market trends.
- `DST.4.3.3.11` Connect branding to target market.
- `DST.4.3.3.12` Explain the 'Unique Selling Point' (USP).
- `DST.4.3.3.13` Construct a market feasibility study.
- `DST.4.3.3.14` Evaluate the saturation of a specific market sector.
- `DST.4.3.3.15` Defend a pricing strategy based on market positioning.
- `DST.4.3.3.16` Synthesize consumer behavior data with product innovation.

##### DST.4.3.4 — Product Analysis (disassembly, evaluating function/aesthetics/cost)

- `DST.4.3.4.1` Identify the parts of a toy (wheels, handle, body).
- `DST.4.3.4.2` Name the materials used in a simple object.
- `DST.4.3.4.3` Recall what an object is used for.
- `DST.4.3.4.4` Observe how parts fit together.
- `DST.4.3.4.5` Disassemble a simple mechanical product safely.
- `DST.4.3.4.6` Explain the function of specific components.
- `DST.4.3.4.7` Compare two similar products (e.g., two different pens).
- `DST.4.3.4.8` Evaluate if a product looks good (Aesthetics).
- `DST.4.3.4.9` Analyze a product using ACCESS FM (Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Size, Safety, Function, Material).
- `DST.4.3.4.10` Interpret how manufacturing methods influence design.
- `DST.4.3.4.11` Connect material choices to the product's cost.
- `DST.4.3.4.12` Explain the concept of 'Reverse Engineering'.
- `DST.4.3.4.13` Construct a comprehensive teardown analysis report.
- `DST.4.3.4.14` Evaluate the 'Value Engineering' of a commercial product.
- `DST.4.3.4.15` Defend a critique of a product's planned obsolescence.
- `DST.4.3.4.16` Synthesize functional analysis with aesthetic theory.

##### DST.4.3.5 — User-Centered Research (identifying needs, empathy mapping, surveys)

- `DST.4.3.5.1` Identify a simple problem that a friend or family member has.
- `DST.4.3.5.2` Ask questions to find out what someone likes or dislikes.
- `DST.4.3.5.3` Observe how people use objects in daily life.
- `DST.4.3.5.4` Draw a picture of a solution for a specific person.
- `DST.4.3.5.5` Conduct a simple survey to gather opinions from a group.
- `DST.4.3.5.6` Explain why we design for others and not just ourselves (empathy).
- `DST.4.3.5.7` Create a list of 'Needs' and 'Wants' for a project.
- `DST.4.3.5.8` Summarize the main problem to be solved.
- `DST.4.3.5.9` Construct an Empathy Map to visualize user feelings and actions.
- `DST.4.3.5.10` Analyze data from questionnaires to inform design choices.
- `DST.4.3.5.11` Identify the 'Primary User' and 'Stakeholders'.
- `DST.4.3.5.12` Explain the importance of inclusive design.
- `DST.4.3.5.13` Construct detailed User Personas based on ethnographic research.
- `DST.4.3.5.14` Evaluate the validity of qualitative vs. quantitative data.
- `DST.4.3.5.15` Defend design decisions based on user-centered evidence.
- `DST.4.3.5.16` Synthesize interview data to define the core 'Pain Points'.

##### DST.4.3.6 — Writing Design Briefs & Specifications (defining measurable success criteria)

- `DST.4.3.6.1` Say what I am going to make.
- `DST.4.3.6.2` Draw what the finished object will look like.
- `DST.4.3.6.3` Name one thing the object must do.
- `DST.4.3.6.4` Recall who the object is for.
- `DST.4.3.6.5` Write a short paragraph describing the project (The Brief).
- `DST.4.3.6.6` List three rules the design must follow (Criteria).
- `DST.4.3.6.7` Explain what 'Constraint' means (limitations).
- `DST.4.3.6.8` Check if the idea matches the description.
- `DST.4.3.6.9` Construct a SMART design specification (Specific, Measurable, etc.).
- `DST.4.3.6.10` Analyze the difference between a Brief (problem) and Spec (rules).
- `DST.4.3.6.11` Identify hard constraints (time, money, size).
- `DST.4.3.6.12` Explain the role of the client in defining the brief.
- `DST.4.3.6.13` Construct a professional technical specification document.
- `DST.4.3.6.14` Evaluate the feasibility of a brief against resources.
- `DST.4.3.6.15` Defend the modification of specifications during the process.
- `DST.4.3.6.16` Synthesize user needs and technical constraints into a coherent scope.

## ELA — Language Arts & Humanities

### ELA.1 — Grammar, Mechanics & Linguistics

#### ELA.1.1 — Introductory Linguistics

##### ELA.1.1.1 — History of the English Language

- `ELA.1.1.1.1` Identify that words change over time.
- `ELA.1.1.1.2` Name "Old English" as the language of Beowulf.
- `ELA.1.1.1.3` Recall that English borrowed words from French and Latin.
- `ELA.1.1.1.4` Observe how Shakespeare’s words look different from ours.
- `ELA.1.1.1.5` Summarize the three main periods: Old, Middle, and Modern English.
- `ELA.1.1.1.6` Explain the impact of the Norman Conquest (1066) on vocabulary.
- `ELA.1.1.1.7` Compare a passage of Chaucer with a modern translation.
- `ELA.1.1.1.8` Identify the Great Vowel Shift.
- `ELA.1.1.1.9` Analyze the influence of the King James Bible on English idioms.
- `ELA.1.1.1.10` Interpret the etymology of common words.
- `ELA.1.1.1.11` Connect global trade to loanwords (e.g., pajama, ketchup).
- `ELA.1.1.1.12` Explain the standardization of spelling (dictionaries).
- `ELA.1.1.1.13` Construct a timeline of the development of English.
- `ELA.1.1.1.14` Evaluate the fluidity of language ("correctness" vs. usage).
- `ELA.1.1.1.15` Defend the beauty of language evolution.
- `ELA.1.1.1.16` Synthesize the Indo-European language family tree.

##### ELA.1.1.2 — Morphology (Roots, Prefixes, Suffixes)

- `ELA.1.1.2.1` Identify a root word inside a bigger word.
- `ELA.1.1.2.2` Add "s" to make plural or "ed" for past.
- `ELA.1.1.2.3` Recall that "un-" means not.
- `ELA.1.1.2.4` Observe how endings change part of speech (quick -> quickly).
- `ELA.1.1.2.5` Summarize the meaning of common Latin roots (e.g., struct, port).
- `ELA.1.1.2.6` Explain the difference between a base word and a root.
- `ELA.1.1.2.7` Break a complex word into morphemes.
- `ELA.1.1.2.8` Identify bound vs. free morphemes.
- `ELA.1.1.2.9` Analyze how prefixes alter meaning (negation, direction, time).
- `ELA.1.1.2.10` Interpret derivational vs. inflectional suffixes.
- `ELA.1.1.2.11` Connect Greek roots to scientific vocabulary.
- `ELA.1.1.2.12` Explain the concept of agglutination (intro).
- `ELA.1.1.2.13` Construct new words using standard morphological rules.
- `ELA.1.1.2.14` Evaluate the clarity of neologisms.
- `ELA.1.1.2.15` Defend the logic of English spelling based on morphology.
- `ELA.1.1.2.16` Synthesize morphological awareness with reading comprehension.

##### ELA.1.1.3 — Phonology (Sounds of Language)

- `ELA.1.1.3.1` Identify rhyming sounds.
- `ELA.1.1.3.2` Clap syllables in a name.
- `ELA.1.1.3.3` Recall that letters represent sounds.
- `ELA.1.1.3.4` Observe how mouth shape changes sound.
- `ELA.1.1.3.5` Summarize the difference between vowels and consonants.
- `ELA.1.1.3.6` Explain phonemes (smallest unit of sound).
- `ELA.1.1.3.7` Compare voiced and unvoiced sounds (b vs. p).
- `ELA.1.1.3.8` Identify dipthongs and blends.
- `ELA.1.1.3.9` Analyze the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) chart (intro).
- `ELA.1.1.3.10` Interpret stress patterns in multi-syllabic words.
- `ELA.1.1.3.11` Connect intonation to meaning (question vs. statement).
- `ELA.1.1.3.12` Explain dialect variations in pronunciation.
- `ELA.1.1.3.13` Construct a phonetic transcription of a simple sentence.
- `ELA.1.1.3.14` Evaluate the difficulty of English phonology for learners.
- `ELA.1.1.3.15` Defend the importance of clear articulation.
- `ELA.1.1.3.16` Synthesize sound patterns with poetic meter.

##### ELA.1.1.4 — Semantics and Pragmatics (Meaning in Context)

- `ELA.1.1.4.1` Identify happy words vs. sad words.
- `ELA.1.1.4.2` Name opposites (antonyms).
- `ELA.1.1.4.3` Recall that "bank" can mean money place or river side.
- `ELA.1.1.4.4` Observe politeness words ("Please").
- `ELA.1.1.4.5` Summarize synonyms (words that mean the same).
- `ELA.1.1.4.6` Explain idiom phrases ("It's raining cats and dogs").
- `ELA.1.1.4.7` Identify sarcasm or implied meaning.
- `ELA.1.1.4.8` Compare literal meaning vs. figurative meaning.
- `ELA.1.1.4.9` Analyze connotation vs. denotation.
- `ELA.1.1.4.10` Interpret speech acts (requests, commands, promises).
- `ELA.1.1.4.11` Connect context to word meaning (Polysemy).
- `ELA.1.1.4.12` Explain ambiguity.
- `ELA.1.1.4.13` Construct sentences with precise semantic nuance.
- `ELA.1.1.4.14` Evaluate how tone changes meaning.
- `ELA.1.1.4.15` Defend the power of words to bless or curse (Proverbs 18:21).
- `ELA.1.1.4.16` Synthesize linguistic theory with effective communication.

#### ELA.1.2 — Parts of Speech and Word Functions

##### ELA.1.2.1 — Adjectives and Adverbs

- `ELA.1.2.1.1` Identify adjectives as words that describe things.
- `ELA.1.2.1.2` Identify adverbs as words that describe actions (often ending in -ly).
- `ELA.1.2.1.3` Use describing words to make sentences more interesting.
- `ELA.1.2.1.4` Sort words into 'Describing a Thing' vs. 'Describing an Action'.
- `ELA.1.2.1.5` Categorize adjectives by what they tell (Which one? What kind? How many?).
- `ELA.1.2.1.6` Form comparative (-er) and superlative (-est) adjectives correctly.
- `ELA.1.2.1.7` Use adverbs to modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs.
- `ELA.1.2.1.8` Distinguish between 'Good' (adjective) and 'Well' (adverb).
- `ELA.1.2.1.9` Analyze the placement of modifiers to avoid confusion.
- `ELA.1.2.1.10` Interpret the use of intensifiers (very, really, quite).
- `ELA.1.2.1.11` Connect predicate adjectives to linking verbs.
- `ELA.1.2.1.12` Explain the order of adjectives (Quantity, Quality, Size, Age, Shape, Color, Origin, Material).
- `ELA.1.2.1.13` Construct sentences with nuanced modification.
- `ELA.1.2.1.14` Evaluate the overuse of adverbs (show, don't tell).
- `ELA.1.2.1.15` Defend the use of a dangling modifier (or correct it).
- `ELA.1.2.1.16` Synthesize adjectival clauses for precise description.

##### ELA.1.2.2 — Function vs. Form

- `ELA.1.2.2.1` Identify that the same word can do different jobs (e.g., 'I *run*' vs. 'A long *run*').
- `ELA.1.2.2.2` Sort words into 'Nouns' and 'Verbs' based on how they are used.
- `ELA.1.2.2.3` Recognize that words have jobs in a sentence.
- `ELA.1.2.2.4` Observe that word order matters.
- `ELA.1.2.2.5` Explain how a word like 'paint' can be a noun or a verb.
- `ELA.1.2.2.6` Identify when a noun is acting like an adjective (e.g., 'chicken' soup).
- `ELA.1.2.2.7` Compare the form of a word with its function.
- `ELA.1.2.2.8` Apply knowledge of parts of speech to fix sentences.
- `ELA.1.2.2.9` Analyze words that function as different parts of speech depending on context.
- `ELA.1.2.2.10` Interpret the function of a word based on its suffix.
- `ELA.1.2.2.11` Connect sentence diagramming to determining function.
- `ELA.1.2.2.12` Explain why dictionaries list multiple parts of speech for one word.
- `ELA.1.2.2.13` Construct sentences where words shift function for rhetorical effect (anthimeria).
- `ELA.1.2.2.14` Evaluate the grammatical correctness of functional shifts.
- `ELA.1.2.2.15` Defend the flexibility of English morphology.
- `ELA.1.2.2.16` Synthesize form and function in linguistic analysis.

##### ELA.1.2.3 — Nouns

- `ELA.1.2.3.1` Identify nouns as names for a person, place, thing, or idea.
- `ELA.1.2.3.2` Distinguish between common (city) and proper (London) nouns.
- `ELA.1.2.3.3` Form plural nouns by adding -s or -es.
- `ELA.1.2.3.4` Capitalize proper nouns in own writing.
- `ELA.1.2.3.5` Categorize nouns as abstract (courage), concrete (rock), or collective (herd).
- `ELA.1.2.3.6` Form possessive nouns correctly (singular and plural).
- `ELA.1.2.3.7` Identify the function of a noun in a sentence (Subject or Object).
- `ELA.1.2.3.8` Use appositives to rename nouns.
- `ELA.1.2.3.9` Analyze the role of nominalization (turning verbs/adjectives into nouns).
- `ELA.1.2.3.10` Interpret the difference between count and non-count nouns.
- `ELA.1.2.3.11` Connect noun usage to subject-verb agreement in complex sentences.
- `ELA.1.2.3.12` Explain the function of a noun clause.
- `ELA.1.2.3.13` Construct sentences using sophisticated nominal structures.
- `ELA.1.2.3.14` Evaluate the stylistic effect of abstract vs. concrete nouns.
- `ELA.1.2.3.15` Defend the capitalization of theological terms based on style guides.
- `ELA.1.2.3.16` Synthesize noun functions within gerund phrases.

##### ELA.1.2.4 — Prepositions and Conjunctions

- `ELA.1.2.4.1` Identify position words (in, on, under, beside).
- `ELA.1.2.4.2` Use 'and', 'but', and 'or' to join words.
- `ELA.1.2.4.3` Recognize that some words connect ideas.
- `ELA.1.2.4.4` Follow instructions with positional words.
- `ELA.1.2.4.5` Identify prepositional phrases in a sentence.
- `ELA.1.2.4.6` Use subordinating conjunctions (because, since, if) to make complex sentences.
- `ELA.1.2.4.7` Explain the object of a preposition.
- `ELA.1.2.4.8` Connect ideas logically using transition words.
- `ELA.1.2.4.9` Analyze the function of correlative conjunctions (either/or, neither/nor).
- `ELA.1.2.4.10` Interpret the difference between a preposition and an adverb.
- `ELA.1.2.4.11` Connect the use of conjunctions to sentence flow.
- `ELA.1.2.4.12` Explain how prepositions show relationships of time and space.
- `ELA.1.2.4.13` Construct complex sentences using varied connective logic.
- `ELA.1.2.4.14` Evaluate the stylistic choice of ending a sentence with a preposition.
- `ELA.1.2.4.15` Defend the use of polysyndeton or asyndeton in rhetoric.
- `ELA.1.2.4.16` Synthesize prepositional phrases acting as adjectives or adverbs.

##### ELA.1.2.5 — Pronouns

- `ELA.1.2.5.1` Identify simple pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they).
- `ELA.1.2.5.2` Replace a name with the correct pronoun.
- `ELA.1.2.5.3` Use 'I' correctly when talking about self.
- `ELA.1.2.5.4` Match pronouns to the person they are talking about.
- `ELA.1.2.5.5` Categorize pronouns by type (Personal, Possessive, Reflexive).
- `ELA.1.2.5.6` Ensure pronouns agree with their antecedents in number and gender.
- `ELA.1.2.5.7` Use relative pronouns (who, which, that) to start clauses.
- `ELA.1.2.5.8` Distinguish between subject pronouns (I) and object pronouns (me).
- `ELA.1.2.5.9` Analyze the case of pronouns (Nominative, Objective, Possessive).
- `ELA.1.2.5.10` Interpret the correct usage of 'Who' vs. 'Whom'.
- `ELA.1.2.5.11` Connect demonstrative pronouns to the pointing function.
- `ELA.1.2.5.12` Explain the function of indefinite pronouns and verb agreement.
- `ELA.1.2.5.13` Construct sentences avoiding ambiguous antecedents.
- `ELA.1.2.5.14` Evaluate the use of the 'editorial we' or formal registers.
- `ELA.1.2.5.15` Defend the grammatical logic of pronoun case in elliptical clauses (e.g., 'taller than I').
- `ELA.1.2.5.16` Synthesize the use of reflexive pronouns for emphasis.

##### ELA.1.2.6 — Verbs

- `ELA.1.2.6.1` Identify verbs as 'doing' words or 'being' words.
- `ELA.1.2.6.2` Change verbs to show past, present, and future (simple tenses).
- `ELA.1.2.6.3` Match verbs to the subject (He runs, They run).
- `ELA.1.2.6.4` Identify helping verbs (is, am, are, was, were).
- `ELA.1.2.6.5` Categorize verbs as Action, Linking, or Helping.
- `ELA.1.2.6.6` Form perfect tenses (have/had + participle) correctly.
- `ELA.1.2.6.7` Use irregular verbs correctly in the past tense.
- `ELA.1.2.6.8` Identify the main verb phrase in a sentence.
- `ELA.1.2.6.9` Analyze the three moods of verbs: Indicative, Imperative, Subjunctive.
- `ELA.1.2.6.10` Interpret the difference between Active and Passive voice.
- `ELA.1.2.6.11` Connect verb aspect (Progressive, Perfect) to the timing of an action.
- `ELA.1.2.6.12` Explain how modal verbs (might, should, must) change meaning.
- `ELA.1.2.6.13` Construct complex sentences maintaining consistent verb tense.
- `ELA.1.2.6.14` Evaluate the rhetorical effect of using the Passive Voice.
- `ELA.1.2.6.15` Defend the use of the Subjunctive Mood for hypothetical situations.
- `ELA.1.2.6.16` Synthesize verb choice to strengthen writing (strong verbs vs. adverbs).

#### ELA.1.3 — Phrases, Clauses & Sentence Structure

##### ELA.1.3.1 — Clause Types (Independent, Dependent, Relative)

- `ELA.1.3.1.1` Identify a complete thought.
- `ELA.1.3.1.2` Name the "Subject" and the "Action".
- `ELA.1.3.1.3` Recall that a sentence needs a capital and a period.
- `ELA.1.3.1.4` Observe sentences joined by "and".
- `ELA.1.3.1.5` Summarize an Independent Clause (can stand alone).
- `ELA.1.3.1.6` Explain a Dependent Clause (needs a helper).
- `ELA.1.3.1.7` Identify subordinate conjunctions (because, if, when).
- `ELA.1.3.1.8` Compare a phrase (no verb) with a clause (has verb).
- `ELA.1.3.1.9` Analyze Relative Clauses (starting with who/which/that).
- `ELA.1.3.1.10` Interpret Noun Clauses acting as subjects or objects.
- `ELA.1.3.1.11` Connect clause variety to writing flow.
- `ELA.1.3.1.12` Explain restrictive vs. non-restrictive clauses (comma usage).
- `ELA.1.3.1.13` Construct sentences using Adverbial Clauses.
- `ELA.1.3.1.14` Evaluate the logic of sentence subordination.
- `ELA.1.3.1.15` Defend the use of complex syntax for complex thoughts.
- `ELA.1.3.1.16` Synthesize clause analysis with sentence diagramming.

##### ELA.1.3.2 — Phrases (Prepositional, Appositive, Verbal)

- `ELA.1.3.2.1` Identify words that tell "where" (in the box).
- `ELA.1.3.2.2` Name a group of words acting together.
- `ELA.1.3.2.3` Recall that phrases don't have a subject doing a verb.
- `ELA.1.3.2.4` Observe extra details in a sentence.
- `ELA.1.3.2.5` Summarize Prepositional Phrases (starts with prep, ends with noun).
- `ELA.1.3.2.6` Explain Appositives (renaming the noun).
- `ELA.1.3.2.7` Identify Participial Phrases (-ing words describing).
- `ELA.1.3.2.8` Use an Infinitive Phrase (to run) as a noun.
- `ELA.1.3.2.9` Analyze the function of a Gerund Phrase (acting as a noun).
- `ELA.1.3.2.10` Interpret how phrases modify other words.
- `ELA.1.3.2.11` Connect phrase placement to clarity (avoiding dangling modifiers).
- `ELA.1.3.2.12` Explain Absolute Phrases.
- `ELA.1.3.2.13` Construct sentences rich with varied phrase types.
- `ELA.1.3.2.14` Evaluate the rhythmic effect of phrases.
- `ELA.1.3.2.15` Defend the stylistic choice of sentence fragments (rarely).
- `ELA.1.3.2.16` Synthesize grammatical function with rhetorical effect.

##### ELA.1.3.3 — Sentence Classifications (Simple, Compound, Complex)

- `ELA.1.3.3.1` Identify a short sentence.
- `ELA.1.3.3.2` Combine two sentences with "and".
- `ELA.1.3.3.3` Recall that we can make long sentences.
- `ELA.1.3.3.4` Observe punctuation rules for joining.
- `ELA.1.3.3.5` Summarize Simple (one idea) vs. Compound (two equal ideas).
- `ELA.1.3.3.6` Explain Complex sentences (one strong, one weak part).
- `ELA.1.3.3.7` Create a Compound-Complex sentence.
- `ELA.1.3.3.8` Identify FANBOYS conjunctions.
- `ELA.1.3.3.9` Analyze sentence variety in a paragraph.
- `ELA.1.3.3.10` Interpret the relationship between clauses in a complex sentence.
- `ELA.1.3.3.11` Connect sentence structure to pacing.
- `ELA.1.3.3.12` Explain run-on sentences and splices.
- `ELA.1.3.3.13` Construct a persuasive paragraph using all four types.
- `ELA.1.3.3.14` Evaluate the impact of short, choppy sentences vs. flowing ones.
- `ELA.1.3.3.15` Defend the need for variety to keep reader interest.
- `ELA.1.3.3.16` Synthesize syntax with logical argumentation.

##### ELA.1.3.4 — Subject-Verb Agreement

- `ELA.1.3.4.1` Identify "He runs" vs. "They run".
- `ELA.1.3.4.2` Match singular nouns to singular verbs.
- `ELA.1.3.4.3` Recall that "is" and "are" change based on who it is.
- `ELA.1.3.4.4` Observe plurals ending in 's' often don't have 's' on the verb.
- `ELA.1.3.4.5` Summarize the basic rule of agreement.
- `ELA.1.3.4.6` Explain compound subjects joined by "and" (usually plural).
- `ELA.1.3.4.7` Handle "or" situations (match the closer subject).
- `ELA.1.3.4.8` Identify collective nouns (team, family) as singular.
- `ELA.1.3.4.9` Analyze agreement with indefinite pronouns (everyone, somebody).
- `ELA.1.3.4.10` Interpret intervening phrases ("The box of apples is heavy").
- `ELA.1.3.4.11` Connect "There is/There are" to the subject that follows.
- `ELA.1.3.4.12` Explain agreement with amounts ($10 is enough).
- `ELA.1.3.4.13` Construct complex sentences with perfect agreement.
- `ELA.1.3.4.14` Evaluate dialect variations vs. standard grammar.
- `ELA.1.3.4.15` Defend the clarity that agreement provides.
- `ELA.1.3.4.16` Synthesize grammar rules with editing skills.

#### ELA.1.4 — Punctuation, Mechanics & Usage

##### ELA.1.4.1 — Capitalization Rules

- `ELA.1.4.1.1` Identify big letters at the start of a sentence.
- `ELA.1.4.1.2` Name "I" as always big.
- `ELA.1.4.1.3` Recall that names of people and places get big letters.
- `ELA.1.4.1.4` Observe titles on books.
- `ELA.1.4.1.5` Summarize capitalizing days, months, and holidays.
- `ELA.1.4.1.6` Explain proper nouns vs. common nouns.
- `ELA.1.4.1.7` Capitalize titles of people (Dr., Mrs., President) correctly.
- `ELA.1.4.1.8` Identify capitalization in titles of works.
- `ELA.1.4.1.9` Analyze the capitalization of Deity pronouns (He/Him for God).
- `ELA.1.4.1.10` Interpret regional capitalizations (North vs. north).
- `ELA.1.4.1.11` Connect capitalization to specific historical events.
- `ELA.1.4.1.12` Explain brand names vs. generic products.
- `ELA.1.4.1.13` Construct a bibliography with correct capitalization.
- `ELA.1.4.1.14` Evaluate poetic license in capitalization (e.g., e.e. cummings).
- `ELA.1.4.1.15` Defend the conventions of standard English.
- `ELA.1.4.1.16` Synthesize style guides (MLA/Chicago) with writing.

##### ELA.1.4.2 — Commas and Semicolons

- `ELA.1.4.2.1` Identify a pause in a sentence.
- `ELA.1.4.2.2` Use commas in a list (apples, bananas, and pears).
- `ELA.1.4.2.3` Recall commas in dates and cities.
- `ELA.1.4.2.4` Observe commas after "Yes" or "No".
- `ELA.1.4.2.5` Summarize using a comma with a conjunction to join sentences.
- `ELA.1.4.2.6` Explain using a semicolon to join related sentences.
- `ELA.1.4.2.7` Use commas to set off introductory phrases.
- `ELA.1.4.2.8` Identify the Oxford Comma debate.
- `ELA.1.4.2.9` Analyze non-essential clauses (set off by commas).
- `ELA.1.4.2.10` Interpret the semicolon as a "soft period".
- `ELA.1.4.2.11` Connect commas to direct address ("John, come here").
- `ELA.1.4.2.12` Explain colon usage for lists or emphasis.
- `ELA.1.4.2.13` Construct complex sentences with precise punctuation.
- `ELA.1.4.2.14` Evaluate the clarity impact of missing punctuation ("Let's eat Grandma").
- `ELA.1.4.2.15` Defend the rules of punctuation as aids to breathing and logic.
- `ELA.1.4.2.16` Synthesize mechanical correctness with flow.

##### ELA.1.4.3 — End Marks and Quotations

- `ELA.1.4.3.1` Identify a period, question mark, and exclamation point.
- `ELA.1.4.3.2` Match the mark to the sentence type.
- `ELA.1.4.3.3` Recall that "talking marks" hug the words spoken.
- `ELA.1.4.3.4` Observe punctuation inside the quotes.
- `ELA.1.4.3.5` Summarize the four sentence types (Declarative, Interrogative, etc.).
- `ELA.1.4.3.6` Explain how to punctuate dialogue.
- `ELA.1.4.3.7` Use single quotes for quotes inside quotes.
- `ELA.1.4.3.8` Identify split quotations.
- `ELA.1.4.3.9` Analyze the placement of periods/commas inside quotes (US standard).
- `ELA.1.4.3.10` Interpret the use of block quotes for long passages.
- `ELA.1.4.3.11` Connect exclamation points to emotion (use sparingly).
- `ELA.1.4.3.12` Explain the ellipsis (...) for omitted words.
- `ELA.1.4.3.13` Construct a dialogue with perfect mechanics.
- `ELA.1.4.3.14` Evaluate the use of the interrobang (?!) or informal marks.
- `ELA.1.4.3.15` Defend the integrity of quoting sources accurately.
- `ELA.1.4.3.16` Synthesize citations with quotation mechanics.

##### ELA.1.4.4 — Usage and Common Errors

- `ELA.1.4.4.1` Identify "a" vs "an".
- `ELA.1.4.4.2` Use "I" instead of "Me" in the subject.
- `ELA.1.4.4.3` Recall double negatives are a no-no.
- `ELA.1.4.4.4` Observe "good" vs "well".
- `ELA.1.4.4.5` Summarize homophone errors (to/two/too).
- `ELA.1.4.4.6` Explain "lie" vs "lay".
- `ELA.1.4.4.7` Distinguish "fewer" (countable) vs "less" (uncountable).
- `ELA.1.4.4.8` Identify misplaced modifiers.
- `ELA.1.4.4.9` Analyze parallel structure in lists.
- `ELA.1.4.4.10` Interpret passive voice vs. active voice.
- `ELA.1.4.4.11` Connect clarity to proper usage.
- `ELA.1.4.4.12` Explain "who" vs "whom".
- `ELA.1.4.4.13` Construct sentences avoiding split infinitives (if adhering to strict style).
- `ELA.1.4.4.14` Evaluate prescriptive vs. descriptive grammar.
- `ELA.1.4.4.15` Defend the standard of excellence in communication.
- `ELA.1.4.4.16` Synthesize editing skills to polish drafts.

#### ELA.1.5 — Syntax and Sentence Diagramming

##### ELA.1.5.1 — Advanced Structures (Verbals and Clauses)

- `ELA.1.5.1.1` Identify action words ending in -ing.
- `ELA.1.5.1.2` Name "To run" as a verb form.
- `ELA.1.5.1.3` Recall that some verb-looking words act like nouns.
- `ELA.1.5.1.4` Observe complex sentences.
- `ELA.1.5.1.5` Summarize Gerunds (nouns), Participles (adjectives), Infinitives (nouns/adj/adv).
- `ELA.1.5.1.6` Explain how to diagram a prepositional phrase on a slant line.
- `ELA.1.5.1.7` Diagram a direct and indirect object.
- `ELA.1.5.1.8` Identify a predicate nominative vs. predicate adjective.
- `ELA.1.5.1.9` Analyze the diagramming of noun clauses on stilts.
- `ELA.1.5.1.10` Interpret the diagramming of compound sentences (dotted line connection).
- `ELA.1.5.1.11` Connect syntax to logical analysis of thought.
- `ELA.1.5.1.12` Explain the objective complement.
- `ELA.1.5.1.13` Construct a diagram for a complex-compound sentence.
- `ELA.1.5.1.14` Evaluate the utility of diagramming for understanding difficult texts.
- `ELA.1.5.1.15` Defend the structure of language as a reflection of logical order.
- `ELA.1.5.1.16` Synthesize grammar mastery with sentence analysis.

##### ELA.1.5.2 — Diagramming Basics (Subject, Predicate, Modifiers)

- `ELA.1.5.2.1` Draw a horizontal line.
- `ELA.1.5.2.2` Separate the Who (Subject) and Did What (Verb) with a vertical line.
- `ELA.1.5.2.3` Recall that describing words hang down.
- `ELA.1.5.2.4` Diagram "Dogs bark."
- `ELA.1.5.2.5` Summarize the baseline of a diagram.
- `ELA.1.5.2.6` Explain where adjectives and adverbs go (slanted lines under).
- `ELA.1.5.2.7` Diagram "The big red dog runs fast."
- `ELA.1.5.2.8` Identify the direct object (vertical line that doesn't cross).
- `ELA.1.5.2.9` Analyze the placement of compound subjects and verbs (rocket ship shape).
- `ELA.1.5.2.10` Interpret the visual representation of sentence logic.
- `ELA.1.5.2.11` Connect parts of speech to their diagram position.
- `ELA.1.5.2.12` Explain the understood "You" in commands.
- `ELA.1.5.2.13` Construct diagrams for sentences with conjunctions.
- `ELA.1.5.2.14` Evaluate why we diagram (to see how words work together).
- `ELA.1.5.2.15` Defend the discipline of sentence analysis.
- `ELA.1.5.2.16` Synthesize basic grammar with visual mapping.

##### ELA.1.5.3 — Syntax Patterns and Style

- `ELA.1.5.3.1` Identify sentences that sound the same.
- `ELA.1.5.3.2` Make a sentence long or short.
- `ELA.1.5.3.3` Recall that variety is interesting.
- `ELA.1.5.3.4` Observe how Yoda talks (weird syntax).
- `ELA.1.5.3.5` Summarize S-V-O (Subject-Verb-Object) order.
- `ELA.1.5.3.6` Explain Inverted Syntax for effect ("Into the room walked the king").
- `ELA.1.5.3.7` Identify loose vs. periodic sentences.
- `ELA.1.5.3.8` Compare active syntax with passive syntax.
- `ELA.1.5.3.9` Analyze the rhetorical effect of sentence length.
- `ELA.1.5.3.10` Interpret parallelism in famous speeches.
- `ELA.1.5.3.11` Connect syntax to authorial voice.
- `ELA.1.5.3.12` Explain balanced sentences.
- `ELA.1.5.3.13` Construct a paragraph demonstrating varied syntax.
- `ELA.1.5.3.14` Evaluate the clarity vs. complexity of a sentence.
- `ELA.1.5.3.15` Defend the choice of syntax to control pacing.
- `ELA.1.5.3.16` Synthesize grammatical correctness with stylistic flair.

### ELA.2 — Humanities Integration (Literature's Context)

#### ELA.2.1 — Cultural Narratives & Worldviews

##### ELA.2.1.1 — How Cultures Tell Their Own Story

- `ELA.2.1.1.1` Identify stories from other countries.
- `ELA.2.1.1.2` Name heroes from different places.
- `ELA.2.1.1.3` Recall that everyone has a story.
- `ELA.2.1.1.4` Observe that people dress and eat differently in stories.
- `ELA.2.1.1.5` Summarize a legend that explains how a country began.
- `ELA.2.1.1.6` Explain why different cultures value different things.
- `ELA.2.1.1.7` Compare an American hero story with a Japanese hero story.
- `ELA.2.1.1.8` Identify what a culture thinks is important.
- `ELA.2.1.1.9` Analyze the 'Founding Myth' of a nation (e.g., Rome's Aeneid vs. America's Pilgrims).
- `ELA.2.1.1.10` Interpret how stories create national identity.
- `ELA.2.1.1.11` Connect cultural narratives to the way people act today.
- `ELA.2.1.1.12` Explain the concept of a 'Counter-Narrative'.
- `ELA.2.1.1.13` Construct a comparison of the metanarratives of Western vs. Eastern civilizations.
- `ELA.2.1.1.14` Evaluate the impact of propaganda in cultural storytelling.
- `ELA.2.1.1.15` Defend the Biblical metanarrative as the true story of the world.
- `ELA.2.1.1.16` Synthesize the role of literature in shaping or reflecting culture.

#### ELA.2.2 — Ethics and Moral Imagination

##### ELA.2.2.1 — Moral Choices in Narrative

- `ELA.2.2.1.1` Identify when a character is kind or mean.
- `ELA.2.2.1.2` Name the helper and the hurter.
- `ELA.2.2.1.3` Recall that we should follow Jesus.
- `ELA.2.2.1.4` Observe that bad choices make sad endings.
- `ELA.2.2.1.5` Summarize a difficult choice a character had to make.
- `ELA.2.2.1.6` Explain what conscience is (the voice inside).
- `ELA.2.2.1.7` Compare what you would do with what the character did.
- `ELA.2.2.1.8` Identify the consequences of a lie.
- `ELA.2.2.1.9` Analyze the complexity of a moral dilemma where there is no easy answer.
- `ELA.2.2.1.10` Interpret the development of a character's conscience.
- `ELA.2.2.1.11` Connect the story to the concept of 'Moral Imagination' (practicing being good).
- `ELA.2.2.1.12` Explain the role of repentance in a character's arc.
- `ELA.2.2.1.13` Construct an ethical critique of a protagonist's decisions.
- `ELA.2.2.1.14` Evaluate the distinction between legal righteousness and true virtue in literature.
- `ELA.2.2.1.15` Defend the need for moral absolutes in storytelling.
- `ELA.2.2.1.16` Synthesize the power of story to shape moral intuition.

#### ELA.2.3 — Literature & History in Conversation

##### ELA.2.3.1 — Historical Novels and Their Contexts

- `ELA.2.3.1.1` Identify that a story happened a long time ago.
- `ELA.2.3.1.2` Name things in the story that we don't have today (e.g., horses instead of cars).
- `ELA.2.3.1.3` Recall that people in history were real people like us.
- `ELA.2.3.1.4` Observe how characters dress and talk.
- `ELA.2.3.1.5` Summarize the historical event behind a story (e.g., The Revolutionary War).
- `ELA.2.3.1.6` Explain what is fact and what is fiction in a historical novel.
- `ELA.2.3.1.7` Compare the story with a history textbook account.
- `ELA.2.3.1.8` Identify how the setting changes the plot.
- `ELA.2.3.1.9` Analyze how the author weaves real history into the narrative.
- `ELA.2.3.1.10` Interpret the accuracy of the historical portrayal.
- `ELA.2.3.1.11` Connect the characters' struggles to the timeline of events.
- `ELA.2.3.1.12` Explain the value of learning history through stories.
- `ELA.2.3.1.13` Construct a critique of a historical novel's fidelity to the era.
- `ELA.2.3.1.14` Evaluate the bias of the author in portraying historical figures.
- `ELA.2.3.1.15` Defend the use of fiction to illuminate historical truth.
- `ELA.2.3.1.16` Synthesize primary source documents with a literary reading of the period.

##### ELA.2.3.2 — Reading Primary Sources as Literature

- `ELA.2.3.2.1` Identify a letter written by someone long ago.
- `ELA.2.3.2.2` Name who wrote it and who read it.
- `ELA.2.3.2.3` Recall that old letters tell us secrets about the past.
- `ELA.2.3.2.4` Listen to a speech from history.
- `ELA.2.3.2.5` Summarize a diary entry from a historical figure.
- `ELA.2.3.2.6` Explain why old writing sounds different.
- `ELA.2.3.2.7` Compare a letter from the Civil War with a modern email.
- `ELA.2.3.2.8` Identify the feelings of the writer.
- `ELA.2.3.2.9` Analyze the rhetorical style of a historical document (e.g., The Gettysburg Address).
- `ELA.2.3.2.10` Interpret the tone and purpose of a primary source.
- `ELA.2.3.2.11` Connect the document to the literature of the same period.
- `ELA.2.3.2.12` Explain the difference between a primary and secondary source.
- `ELA.2.3.2.13` Construct a literary analysis of a non-literary text (e.g., The Magna Carta or The Federalist Papers).
- `ELA.2.3.2.14` Evaluate the worldview assumptions in a primary document.
- `ELA.2.3.2.15` Defend the importance of reading original sources over summaries.
- `ELA.2.3.2.16` Synthesize the literary voice of an era through its documents.

#### ELA.2.4 — Literature & Philosophy

##### ELA.2.4.1 — Big Questions in Story

- `ELA.2.4.1.1` Identify if a character is good or bad.
- `ELA.2.4.1.2` Name the right thing to do in the story.
- `ELA.2.4.1.3` Recall that God wants us to be kind.
- `ELA.2.4.1.4` Ask 'Why did they do that?'
- `ELA.2.4.1.5` Summarize the moral lesson of a fable or story.
- `ELA.2.4.1.6` Explain what the characters believe about right and wrong.
- `ELA.2.4.1.7` Compare a wise choice with a foolish choice.
- `ELA.2.4.1.8` Identify the 'Big Idea' (e.g., Friendship, Courage).
- `ELA.2.4.1.9` Analyze the ethical dilemma faced by a protagonist.
- `ELA.2.4.1.10` Interpret the author's answer to 'What is the good life?'.
- `ELA.2.4.1.11` Connect the story to biblical truth.
- `ELA.2.4.1.12` Explain how ideas have consequences in the plot.
- `ELA.2.4.1.13` Construct an analysis of the philosophical underpinnings of a novel (e.g., Existentialism in Camus).
- `ELA.2.4.1.14` Evaluate the consistency of the author's worldview.
- `ELA.2.4.1.15` Defend a biblical answer to the philosophical questions raised.
- `ELA.2.4.1.16` Synthesize literature as a testing ground for philosophical ideas.

#### ELA.2.5 — Literature, Art & Music Connections

##### ELA.2.5.1 — Shared Themes Across the Arts

- `ELA.2.5.1.1` Identify a picture that matches a story.
- `ELA.2.5.1.2` Name a song that feels like the book.
- `ELA.2.5.1.3` Recall that people paint and write about the same things.
- `ELA.2.5.1.4` Observe colors that show feelings like words do.
- `ELA.2.5.1.5` Summarize how a painting tells a story.
- `ELA.2.5.1.6` Explain how music can make a story scary or happy.
- `ELA.2.5.1.7` Compare a poem about spring with a painting of spring.
- `ELA.2.5.1.8` Identify the mood in both art and text.
- `ELA.2.5.1.9` Analyze the relationship between Romantic poetry and Romantic painting.
- `ELA.2.5.1.10` Interpret the term 'Ekphrasis' (writing about art).
- `ELA.2.5.1.11` Connect a musical era (e.g., Baroque) to its literature.
- `ELA.2.5.1.12` Explain how different art forms express the 'Spirit of the Age'.
- `ELA.2.5.1.13` Construct a comparative essay on a theme (e.g., War) in literature, art, and music.
- `ELA.2.5.1.14` Evaluate the concept of the 'Gesamtkunstwerk' (Total Art Work).
- `ELA.2.5.1.15` Defend the unity of truth, goodness, and beauty across disciplines.
- `ELA.2.5.1.16` Synthesize the cultural output of a specific historical period.

### ELA.3 — Journalism & Nonfiction Writing

#### ELA.3.1 — Ethics in Journalism

##### ELA.3.1.1 — Avoiding Slander and Gossip

- `ELA.3.1.1.1` Identify unkind words.
- `ELA.3.1.1.2` Name gossip as telling secrets that hurt people.
- `ELA.3.1.1.3` Recall that words can hurt like sticks and stones.
- `ELA.3.1.1.4` Observe that we should speak helpful words.
- `ELA.3.1.1.5` Summarize the damage caused by rumors.
- `ELA.3.1.1.6` Explain the difference between reporting news and spreading gossip.
- `ELA.3.1.1.7` Compare private information with public information.
- `ELA.3.1.1.8` Apply the 'THINK' test (True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind).
- `ELA.3.1.1.9` Analyze the legal concepts of Libel (written) and Slander (spoken).
- `ELA.3.1.1.10` Interpret the biblical warnings against the tongue (James 3).
- `ELA.3.1.1.11` Connect privacy rights to ethical reporting.
- `ELA.3.1.1.12` Explain the harm of 'Sensationalism'.
- `ELA.3.1.1.13` Construct an argument for ethical boundaries in reporting.
- `ELA.3.1.1.14` Evaluate the morality of paparazzi and invasion of privacy.
- `ELA.3.1.1.15` Defend the reputation of others as a form of love.
- `ELA.3.1.1.16` Synthesize legal constraints with moral obligations.

##### ELA.3.1.2 — Truth-Telling and Accuracy

- `ELA.3.1.2.1` Identify a lie vs. the truth.
- `ELA.3.1.2.2` Name honesty as a good trait.
- `ELA.3.1.2.3` Recall that God hates lying lips.
- `ELA.3.1.2.4` Check if the story is right.
- `ELA.3.1.2.5` Summarize why facts must be checked.
- `ELA.3.1.2.6` Explain what happens when newspapers make mistakes (Corrections).
- `ELA.3.1.2.7` Compare a rumor with a verified fact.
- `ELA.3.1.2.8` Apply the Ninth Commandment (False Witness) to writing.
- `ELA.3.1.2.9` Analyze the consequences of 'Fake News'.
- `ELA.3.1.2.10` Interpret the concept of verification (two sources).
- `ELA.3.1.2.11` Connect accuracy to trust.
- `ELA.3.1.2.12` Explain the pressure to be 'first' vs. being 'right'.
- `ELA.3.1.2.13` Construct a fact-checking protocol.
- `ELA.3.1.2.14` Evaluate the ethical failure of fabrication (e.g., Stephen Glass).
- `ELA.3.1.2.15` Defend the pursuit of objective truth in a post-truth culture.
- `ELA.3.1.2.16` Synthesize the Christian duty to testify to the truth.

#### ELA.3.2 — Feature Writing & Human Interest Stories

##### ELA.3.2.1 — Narrative Techniques in Nonfiction

- `ELA.3.2.1.1` Tell a true story like a storybook.
- `ELA.3.2.1.2` Describe what the person looks like.
- `ELA.3.2.1.3` Share how the person felt.
- `ELA.3.2.1.4` Make the beginning exciting.
- `ELA.3.2.1.5` Use descriptive language (show, don't just tell).
- `ELA.3.2.1.6` Explain the setting of the true story.
- `ELA.3.2.1.7` Compare a news report (facts) with a feature story (feelings/details).
- `ELA.3.2.1.8` Identify the 'Angle' of the story.
- `ELA.3.2.1.9` Analyze the use of dialogue to bring scenes to life.
- `ELA.3.2.1.10` Interpret the narrative arc of a real-life event.
- `ELA.3.2.1.11` Connect the individual's story to a larger theme.
- `ELA.3.2.1.12` Explain the concept of 'Creative Nonfiction' (true but artistic).
- `ELA.3.2.1.13` Construct a profile piece using immersion journalism techniques.
- `ELA.3.2.1.14` Evaluate the pacing of a long-form feature.
- `ELA.3.2.1.15` Defend the use of literary devices in journalism.
- `ELA.3.2.1.16` Synthesize facts and atmosphere to create empathy.

##### ELA.3.2.2 — Profiles of People

- `ELA.3.2.2.1` Draw a picture of a community helper.
- `ELA.3.2.2.2` Write three things about what they do.
- `ELA.3.2.2.3` Ask them why they like their job.
- `ELA.3.2.2.4` Share their story with the class.
- `ELA.3.2.2.5` Write a biography sketch of a family member.
- `ELA.3.2.2.6` Explain why this person is interesting.
- `ELA.3.2.2.7` Capture a specific moment in their life.
- `ELA.3.2.2.8` Describe their personality, not just their looks.
- `ELA.3.2.2.9` Analyze what makes a person 'newsworthy'.
- `ELA.3.2.2.10` Interpret the subject's words to find their motivation.
- `ELA.3.2.2.11` Connect the person's work to the community's needs.
- `ELA.3.2.2.12` Explain the 'Nut Graf' (why we are reading this now).
- `ELA.3.2.2.13` Construct a psychological profile based on interview and observation.
- `ELA.3.2.2.14` Evaluate the balance between praise and honest critique.
- `ELA.3.2.2.15` Defend the dignity of the subject (Imago Dei) in the writing.
- `ELA.3.2.2.16` Synthesize the person's past, present, and future into a cohesive narrative.

#### ELA.3.3 — Interviewing & Information Gathering

##### ELA.3.3.1 — Listening and Note-Taking

- `ELA.3.3.1.1` Look at the person talking.
- `ELA.3.3.1.2` Wait until they finish to speak.
- `ELA.3.3.1.3` Draw what they said.
- `ELA.3.3.1.4` Repeat what they said to check.
- `ELA.3.3.1.5` Write down key words while listening.
- `ELA.3.3.1.6` Summarize the main point of the speaker.
- `ELA.3.3.1.7` Use a recording device (with permission) to help remember.
- `ELA.3.3.1.8` Identify the most interesting quote.
- `ELA.3.3.1.9` Analyze the difference between verbatim quotes and paraphrasing.
- `ELA.3.3.1.10` Interpret body language and tone during an interview.
- `ELA.3.3.1.11` Connect active listening to building rapport.
- `ELA.3.3.1.12` Explain the importance of accuracy in quotes.
- `ELA.3.3.1.13` Construct a transcript of a recorded interview.
- `ELA.3.3.1.14` Evaluate the speaker's reliability or bias during the interview.
- `ELA.3.3.1.15` Defend the integrity of the subject's intent when editing quotes.
- `ELA.3.3.1.16` Synthesize interview notes into a coherent narrative.
