- `SCI.6.2.4.11` Connect the Reformation to the scientific revolution.
- `SCI.6.2.4.12` Explain the Royal Society's motto ("Nullius in verba" - take nobody's word).
- `SCI.6.2.4.13` Construct a biography of a faithful scientist (Pascal, Boyle, Faraday).
- `SCI.6.2.4.14` Evaluate the Scopes Trial narrative.
- `SCI.6.2.4.15` Defend the thesis that Christianity birthed science.
- `SCI.6.2.4.16` Synthesize historical context with scientific development.

#### SCI.6.3 — Scientific Method & Thinking

##### SCI.6.3.1 — Analyzing Results & Peer Review

- `SCI.6.3.1.1` Decide if my guess was right.
- `SCI.6.3.1.2` Tell others what I found.
- `SCI.6.3.1.3` Listen to what my friends found.
- `SCI.6.3.1.4` Ask 'Did we get the same answer?'
- `SCI.6.3.1.5` Summarize what the data tells us.
- `SCI.6.3.1.6` Explain if the hypothesis was supported or rejected.
- `SCI.6.3.1.7` Compare my results with another group's results.
- `SCI.6.3.1.8` Identify why results might be different.
- `SCI.6.3.1.9` Analyze the sources of error in the experiment.
- `SCI.6.3.1.10` Interpret the relationship between variables (direct/inverse).
- `SCI.6.3.1.11` Connect the conclusion back to the original question.
- `SCI.6.3.1.12` Explain the importance of Peer Review (scientists checking each other).
- `SCI.6.3.1.13` Construct a formal lab report (Abstract, Method, Data, Conclusion).
- `SCI.6.3.1.14` Evaluate the validity of a scientific claim based on methodology.
- `SCI.6.3.1.15` Defend a conclusion using statistical evidence.
- `SCI.6.3.1.16` Synthesize the collaborative nature of the scientific community.

##### SCI.6.3.2 — Asking Good Questions

- `SCI.6.3.2.1` Ask 'Why?' about things in nature.
- `SCI.6.3.2.2` Wonder what will happen if we change something.
- `SCI.6.3.2.3` Choose a question we can answer by looking or testing.
- `SCI.6.3.2.4` Recall that scientists are curious.
- `SCI.6.3.2.5` Formulate a question that can be tested (Testable Question).
- `SCI.6.3.2.6` Distinguish between a question about facts vs. opinions.
- `SCI.6.3.2.7` Predict the answer (Hypothesis) using 'I think... because...'.
- `SCI.6.3.2.8` Explain why we need to ask clear questions.
- `SCI.6.3.2.9` Analyze a problem to identify the variables involved.
- `SCI.6.3.2.10` Construct a Null Hypothesis (no change) and an Alternative Hypothesis.
- `SCI.6.3.2.11` Critique a question that is too vague to be tested.
- `SCI.6.3.2.12` Connect the research question to existing knowledge.
- `SCI.6.3.2.13` Construct a complex research proposal based on a gap in literature.
- `SCI.6.3.2.14` Evaluate the falsifiability of a hypothesis (Popper).
- `SCI.6.3.2.15` Defend the necessity of operational definitions in research questions.
- `SCI.6.3.2.16` Synthesize multiple observations to form a novel hypothesis.

##### SCI.6.3.3 — Collecting and Organizing Data

- `SCI.6.3.3.1` Count things and use tally marks.
- `SCI.6.3.3.2` Draw a picture of the result.
- `SCI.6.3.3.3` Sort items into groups.
- `SCI.6.3.3.4` Measure with a ruler or cup.
- `SCI.6.3.3.5` Create a data table to record numbers.
- `SCI.6.3.3.6` Use a bar graph to show results.
- `SCI.6.3.3.7` Take accurate measurements using standard units.
- `SCI.6.3.3.8` Label drawings with scientific names.
- `SCI.6.3.3.9` Analyze data for patterns and trends.
- `SCI.6.3.3.10` Construct line graphs for continuous data.
- `SCI.6.3.3.11` Calculate the mean, median, and mode of results.
- `SCI.6.3.3.12` Identify outliers (results that don't fit).
- `SCI.6.3.3.13` Construct a scatter plot with a line of best fit.
- `SCI.6.3.3.14` Evaluate the statistical significance of data (Standard Deviation).
- `SCI.6.3.3.15` Defend the integrity of data handling (no cherry-picking).
- `SCI.6.3.3.16` Synthesize error bars and uncertainty in data presentation.

##### SCI.6.3.4 — Designing Experiments

- `SCI.6.3.4.1` Plan a simple test (e.g., which ball bounces higher).
- `SCI.6.3.4.2` Identify what we will change and what we will keep the same.
- `SCI.6.3.4.3` Follow a recipe or list of steps.
- `SCI.6.3.4.4` Use safe hands when testing.
- `SCI.6.3.4.5` Identify the Independent Variable (what I change) and Dependent Variable (what I measure).
- `SCI.6.3.4.6` Explain why we need a 'Fair Test' (Controls).
- `SCI.6.3.4.7` Write a step-by-step procedure.
- `SCI.6.3.4.8` List the materials needed for an experiment.
- `SCI.6.3.4.9` Analyze an experimental design for flaws or bias.
- `SCI.6.3.4.10` Interpret the role of a Control Group vs. Experimental Group.
- `SCI.6.3.4.11` Connect sample size to the reliability of the test.
- `SCI.6.3.4.12` Explain how to minimize human error.
- `SCI.6.3.4.13` Construct a double-blind experiment protocol (if applicable).
- `SCI.6.3.4.14` Evaluate the ethics of an experimental design.
- `SCI.6.3.4.15` Defend the reproducibility of the method.
- `SCI.6.3.4.16` Synthesize multiple variables using multivariate analysis concepts.

##### SCI.6.3.5 — Observation vs Inference

- `SCI.6.3.5.1` Identify what I see with my eyes (Observation).
- `SCI.6.3.5.2` Name a guess about what happened (Inference).
- `SCI.6.3.5.3` Recall that we need to look closely.
- `SCI.6.3.5.4` Describe an object using color, shape, and size.
- `SCI.6.3.5.5` Summarize the difference: Observation is a fact, Inference is an explanation.
- `SCI.6.3.5.6` Explain that 'The ground is wet' is an observation, 'It rained' is an inference.
- `SCI.6.3.5.7` Compare qualitative data (words) with quantitative data (numbers).
- `SCI.6.3.5.8` Record observations accurately without guessing.
- `SCI.6.3.5.9` Analyze how prior knowledge influences inference.
- `SCI.6.3.5.10` Interpret data points without jumping to conclusions.
- `SCI.6.3.5.11` Connect observation to the concept of empirical evidence.
- `SCI.6.3.5.12` Explain the danger of bias in observation.
- `SCI.6.3.5.13` Construct an argument separating raw data from theoretical interpretation.
- `SCI.6.3.5.14` Evaluate historical science (inference-heavy) vs. operational science (observation-heavy).
- `SCI.6.3.5.15` Defend the objectivity of data collection.
- `SCI.6.3.5.16` Synthesize observations to support or reject a theory.

#### SCI.6.4 — Tools, Measurement & Lab Skills

- `SCI.6.4.1.1` Identify measuring carefully.
- `SCI.6.4.1.2` Name the right number.
- `SCI.6.4.1.3` Recall that we check our work.
- `SCI.6.4.1.4` Try again if we mess up.

- `SCI.6.4.1.7` Compare 'Close enough' with 'Exact'.
- `SCI.6.4.1.8` Identify human error (reading the ruler wrong).
- `SCI.6.4.1.9` Analyze the difference between Accuracy (correctness) and Precision (repeatability).
- `SCI.6.4.1.10` Interpret the meniscus when measuring liquid volume.
- `SCI.6.4.1.11` Connect significant figures to the precision of the tool.
- `SCI.6.4.1.12` Explain systematic vs. random error.
- `SCI.6.4.1.13` Construct an error analysis for a lab experiment.
- `SCI.6.4.1.14` Evaluate the % Error of a result.
- `SCI.6.4.1.15` Defend the appropriate number of significant figures in a calculation.
- `SCI.6.4.1.16` Synthesize the concept of uncertainty in all measurement.
